At the edge of my neighborhood, a narrow footbridge crosses a creek that is barely visible in summer. Reeds lean over it, and the water moves beneath them with the patient sound of someone turning pages. Most people use the bridge as a shortcut to the grocery store. I used to do the same.

One autumn morning, I stopped because a child had lined up six yellow leaves along the railing. They were arranged from smallest to largest, each stem pointing toward the water. Nothing about the display was permanent; the next breeze would undo it. Still, someone had taken the time to notice differences among the leaves and give them an order.

After that, I began finding reasons to pause. In winter, the creek carried thin plates of ice that bumped gently against the stones. In spring, a pair of ducks investigated a shopping cart half buried in the mud. By June, the reeds had grown so tall that the bridge felt like a passage through a green room.

The grocery store has not moved, and the walk takes no less time. I still arrive with a list and leave carrying things I will soon use up. But I have learned to look over the railing, even when I expect nothing new. Some days I see only water. Some days I notice a leaf caught in a spider’s web, trembling above the current. I never know which it will be until I stop, and that small uncertainty makes the ordinary walk feel worth taking again.
